newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST - C-C Amatil yr net seen flat.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - C-C Amatil yr net seen flat.

text.p: Softdrink bottler Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd is expected to report a flat full-year profit result on Friday, as it feels the effects of its aggressive expansion and a soft domestic market.
Analysts are forecasting a net profit before abnormals of A$138 million to A$146 million for calender 1996, compared with a net profit of A$138.6 million in 1995.
"The month of December was unseasonably cool and could even have pushed them a little below their forecasts, but I doubt they are going to exceed it," said one Sydney-based analyst.
Forecasts for C-C Amatil, the world's second largest Coca-Cola bottler, were downgraded sharply in mid-November when the company warned its net profit would show little change on 1995.
This contrasted with earlier predictions by the company of percentage profit growth in the "mid-teens", and wiped more than A$2 billion from its market capitalisation.
A star performer of the Australian share market since mid-1995, C-C Amatil's share price slumped from A$17.54 on November 15 to a low of A$12.45.
The share price closed on Wednesday at A$13.30.
Analysts said there were concerns about a price discount war with rival Pepsi Cola as well as a weak domestic market, and growth forecasts had been flattened for the next two years.

"The perception among Coca-Cola Amatil investors is that the domestic company been funding the expansion of the parent company in the States by putting in all the capital expenditure and wearing the losses from the market share battle," said Mercantile Mutual executive director Australian equities Greg Matthews.
C-C Amatil, which is about 36 percent owned by Coca-Cola Co, invested about A$800 million in plant and other capital items in 1996 and increased its employees to 25,000 from 18,000.
Little pick-up in earnings was expected over the next two years given the demands of ongoing expansion into Asia and eastern Europe, said one Sydney-based analyst.
"They will be spending about A$1 billion a year and that takes a lot of financing. It also takes a lot out of cash flow and the rest of their operations in terms of effort," the analyst said.

Another Sydney-based analyst suggested the market might also focus on earnings per share, which would be significantly lower than in 1995 due a stock placement to Malaysian tycoon Robert Kuok's Kerry Group.
The September placement of 46.0 million shares, representing 9.275 percent of stock, was made at A$14.51 a share.

However, Matthews noted that C-C Amatil's share price was on about 45 times earnings, compared with an average industrial price-earnings ratio of about 16. "That's still a pretty big vote of confidence in management," he said.
